div.head: Ine 16
div.ab: Se ðe ðeof ofslihð, se mot gecyþan mid his aðe, þæt he hine synnigne ofsloge, nallæs ða gegildan.
LX. Se ðe ðeof ofslihð, se mot gecyðan mid aðe, þæt he hine synnigne ofsloge, nalles ða gegildan.
Qui furem occiderit, debet inueritare cum iuramento, quod illum culpabilem (et de uita forisfactum) occidisset, et non soluat.
{LX} Se ðe ðeof ofslihð, se mot gecyðan mid aðe þæt he hine synnigne ofsloge; nalles ða gegildan.
He who kills a thief may declare with an oath that he killed him because he was [found] guilty [in the act]; this does not apply to his associates.
He who kills a thief shall be allowed to declare on oath that the man he slew was guilty. The associates of the slain man shall not be allowed to proceed to an oath.
He who slays a thief may declare with an oath that he slew him as a guilty man, by no means the associates.

Wer einen [handhaften] Dieb erschlägt, der darf [wenn deshalb verklagt,] durch (seinen) Eid erweisen, dass er ihn als Schuldigen erschlagen habe, keineswegs die Gildegenossen [des Todten gelangen zum Beweise].
Whoever slays a [red-handed] thief may [if accused on that account] prove by (his) oath that he slew him as a guilty man; by no means [do] the guild-brothers [of the dead man get to the proof].
div.note: This obscure statement probably means that the thief’s associates have no right to swear to his innocence. These associates (gegildan) have been variously interpreted. Liebermann thinks that already we have a guild like that in VI Athelstan (see No. 37); he notes that in Inc 21, 21.1, the term seems to interchange with “kinsmen”, but suggests that the latter word is being used widely. But it may be gegildan which is vague, denoting “those associated with him in payment” (Attenborough), primarily his kinsmen, see p. 365.
